The paper presents a new approach to calculate the polarimetric radar cross section of canonical targets under SAR geometry.

The scattering mechanism of the object in the far field can be modeled as a linear transformation between the incident electric fields and the scattered electric fields, described by a scattering matrix.
The radar cross section is defined as the effective surface which describes the electromagnetic reflectivity of the target in the direction back to the radar.
The new approach converts the electric field components calculated in the spherical coordinate system into the electric field components in the Cartesian coordinate system.
The three canonical targets considered are the flat plate, the dihedral reflector, and the trihedral reflector.
The maximum value of the radar cross section for the flat plate in the hh polarization is -19.58 dBsm.
The maximum value of the radar cross section for the dihedral reflector in the hh polarization is -13.56 dBsm.
The maximum value of the radar cross section for the trihedral reflector in the hh polarization is -12.54 dBsm.
The SAR geometry has a large effect on the radar backscatter cross section due to the continuously changing angle of the incident and scattered waves.
Trihedral corner reflectors are commonly used as calibration targets or as reference points in radar remote sensing.
The paper mentions the need for improved simulation methods and target modelling for better accuracy and simulation efficiency of the radar cross section.
The authors use physical optics approximation and far-field radiation to determine the polarimetric radar cross section.
The paper presents the simulation results for the flat plate, the dihedral reflector, and the trihedral reflector in different polarization modes.
The authors note that the difference between the scattering maxima of each target conforms with standard theory, confirming the validity of the calculations.
The paper provides a review of electric field in wave propagation, radar cross section, and simulation of scattered fields using physical optics.
